lede: From the Turkish raids on Byzantine Armenia to the Komnenian recovery, and then the long afterlife. The entries for 1071 follow Attaleiates and link into his text; the other dates are those of the modern accounts, and say so where the sources differ.

stations.text: Turkish raids reach Byzantine Armenia: Artze, the great unwalled market town near Theodosiopolis, is sacked in 1049; Alp Arslan takes Ani, the old Armenian royal city, in 1064. Theodosiopolis is walled against 'the Turks' unexpected neighbourhood'.

The empress Eudokia Makrembolitissa becomes regent for her sons, the eldest Michael, under an oath not to remarry. The Caesar John Doukas, the late emperor's brother, and the philosopher Psellos guard the family's interest.

Eudokia breaks her oath and marries Romanos Diogenes, a Cappadocian general lately condemned for conspiracy. He becomes senior emperor beside her three sons: a soldier on the throne of a family that did not choose him. Psellos, woken to hear of it, is taken upstairs with the empress to tell her son.
Romanos campaigns in Syria (Hierapolis taken, 1068) and in Cappadocia and on the Euphrates (1069), with a mercenary army; Turkish raiders slip past him and sack Iconium.

stations.titel: A year at home, and Manzikert lost
stations.text: Romanos stays in the capital on his counsellors' advice and sends Manuel Komnenos east; the Blachernai church, home of the icon that went on campaign, burns to the ground. Manuel is beaten and taken near Sebasteia, the Turks sack Chonai and its pilgrimage church, and the Turkish victor comes over to the emperor with his prisoner. The sultan takes Manzikert, 'the previous year', as Attaleiates says; Matthew of Edessa has the town taken in a day and its people killed.

The sultan's war is for the Abbasid caliph against Fatimid Egypt: Aleppo changes its Friday sermon to Baghdad, and he besieges it anyway until its lord comes out by night with his mother. Before that he spent fifty days before Edessa in vain. Hearing that the emperor is marching east, he turns north with the troops he has to hand.

The court is paid its roga and the army crosses to Asia on the Sunday of Orthodoxy. A dark dove settles in the emperor's hands; the tent falls at Helenopolis, 'the pitiful city'; a fire burns his best horses. In Italy Bari, the last Byzantine city, falls to Robert Guiscard in April.

On the march east the emperor lets his soldiers sack Sebasteia on the word of accusers, drives off the Armenian princes Adom and Abusahl, and swears to destroy the Armenian faith on his return; the monks pray that he should die like Julian. The Byzantine eyewitness does not mention it.

Two months' food for a march through a country 'trampled by the nations'. The Uzes and Roussel's Franks are sent ahead to Khliat, then the larger and better part of the army under Joseph Trachaneiotes; the emperor goes on to Manzikert.

The Armenian infantry storm the outer wall; the Turkish garrison surrenders and comes out armed before an unarmoured emperor. A soldier who stole a donkey loses his nose before the icon of the Virgin: 'then, then indeed, I foresaw a great retribution'.

Foragers attacked, Bryennios repulsed, Basilakes taken, a night of arrows round a camp without moon, the river cut off, an Uze contingent under Tamis gone over. Trachaneiotes, hearing of the sultan, retreats into Roman territory with half the army.

The sultan's envoys offer peace and are refused. Romanos advances all day against a retreating enemy; at evening he turns the imperial standard for the camp; the rear breaks, 'as most people assert' at the word of a cousin of the emperor's stepson; the emperor fights on foot until he is taken. Bryennios, writing for Andronikos' daughter, has the rear simply 'withdraw'.

stations.titel: Eight days as the sultan's guest
stations.text: 'Do not be afraid, emperor', in Attaleiates; three blows and then the pardon, in Ibn al-Athīr; chains and then brotherhood sealed in blood, in Matthew of Edessa. The question ('What would you have done?'), a treaty, a marriage alliance, and release. Ibn al-Athīr names a ransom of a million and a half dinars and a fifty years' truce; Attaleiates only 'a generous gift'.

The empress, despairing of her husband's release, calls in the Caesar John Doukas and orders the provinces not to receive Romanos; the Caesar turns the plan against her, has Michael VII proclaimed sole emperor and sends Eudokia, shorn, to a convent on the Bosporus. Ibn al-Athīr has the deposed emperor offer Michael the choice of honouring the treaty, and send the sultan what money he had. Psellos claims the advice not to receive Romanos back as his own.

Romanos holds Dokeia; his Cappadocian commander Alyates is beaten and blinded after Crispin, whom Romanos had exiled, speaks to the Franks in their own tongue. The Armenian Khatchatour of Antioch comes over; Romanos winters in Cilicia, Andronikos Doukas comes through the Taurus unopposed, and Adana is besieged. Romanos surrenders on the guarantee of three bishops, is blinded at Kotyaion in the summer of 1072, and dies of the wounds on the island of Prote; Eudokia buries him. Psellos says Michael did not know; Bryennios that Andronikos protested. The treaty he made with the sultan is never carried out.

The sultan is stabbed by the commander of a fortress he had besieged across the Oxus. In Matthew of Edessa he had declared the peace broken when he heard of the blinding; the Turkmen move into Anatolia without either treaty or sultan.

Roussel de Bailleul, the Frankish captain of 1071, revolts and is fought with Turkish help; Byzantine pretenders hire Turkish troops and garrison cities with them. By 1081 a Seljuk prince holds Nicaea, and Alexios Komnenos takes the throne.
The judge who rode with the army writes his history for Nikephoros III Botaneiates, who had risen against the Doukai. It is the only eyewitness account of the battle from either side.
French manuscripts of Boccaccio's Fall of Illustrious Men show the emperor as the sultan's footstool or mounting block: the Western legend, far from what the eyewitness saw.
Chapter 57 of the Decline and Fall makes Alp Arslan's clemency and Romanos' fall a set piece of the European canon.
Fernand Grenard photographs the ruins of the fortress of Malazgirt above the village after the earthquake of 30 April.

In modern Turkey the date is commemorated at Malazgirt each year as the opening of Anatolia to the Turks; in Byzantine history it has long served as the beginning of decline. The eyewitness thought the civil war that followed was the worse calamity.
